name: Risk-Adjusted Returns
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why Quantum Bets Need a Higher Hurdle Than Everything Else in the Portfolio
lesson.summary: The discount rate used in NPV should reflect how risky a project actually is, and applying an honest, higher rate to quantum computing reveals how much a comfortable corporate-average rate has been flattering the numbers.
lesson.body:
The discount rate inside an NPV calculation is not an arbitrary input, it should reflect the riskiness of the specific cash flows being discounted, not a company-wide average cost of capital borrowed from safer, more established business lines. Safer, more certain projects deserve a rate close to the risk-free rate, historically in the low single digits for government bonds. Riskier, more uncertain ventures deserve a rate loaded with a risk premium that reflects the real chance the promised cash flows never show up at all.

Quantum computing R&D sits at the risky end of nearly any corporate project portfolio: unproven hardware roadmaps, genuinely uncertain timing for commercial advantage, dependence on error-correction breakthroughs that may or may not arrive on schedule, and a real possibility that the specific approach a company bet on, a particular qubit modality, say, gets superseded before it ever reaches commercial scale. Venture capital investing in early-stage, high-uncertainty technology has historically demanded required returns somewhere in the 25 to 40 percent range or higher, far above the high single digits or low teens typically used for mature, proven capital projects, precisely to compensate for how often such bets return nothing.

Return to the pharmaceutical NPV example from the previous chapter: $4,000,000 per year in years five through eight against a $10,000,000 initial cost. At a 12 percent discount rate, NPV came out to negative $2,278,838, already unattractive. Now apply a more honest, risk-adjusted rate for an unproven quantum application, 25 percent: year five is worth $1,310,720 today, year six is worth $1,048,576, year seven is worth $838,861, and year eight is worth $671,089. Summed, those four flows total $3,869,245. NPV equals $3,869,245 minus $10,000,000, or negative $6,130,755.

The gap between the two results, negative $2,278,838 at a comfortable 12 percent versus negative $6,130,755 at an honestly risk-adjusted 25 percent, is a swing of roughly $3,851,900, driven entirely by being honest about risk rather than by changing a single assumption about the underlying technology. This is the single most common way quantum computing investment cases get flattered internally: borrowing a corporate-average discount rate from stable, proven business lines to evaluate a venture-stage technology bet, which systematically understates how much value is actually being destroyed, or how much return would actually be required to justify the risk taken.

Risk adjustment does not mean quantum computing investment is irrational. Plenty of individually negative-NPV bets are still worth making as part of a diversified portfolio, which is precisely the logic behind venture capital and the subject of the next chapter's expected value framework. It means each project needs to be judged against a discount rate matching its own risk, not the company's safest line of business, and by that honest standard, most quantum computing business cases pitched today would not clear the bar standing alone.
